855.title: Edmund Campion and Margaret Clitherow
855.hook: English Catholics executed for their faith under Elizabeth I
855.howItsDone: Catholics honor Edmund Campion and Margaret Clitherow among the canonized martyrs of England and Wales, and some old English houses still show visitors their hidden priest holes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter Canisius and his little books of questions and answers. Your line was simple words. What did you manage to say plainly? Today, a time when saying it at all could cost your life. Day eight hundred fifty-five.

A knock at the door of a house in York. Somewhere in the house there's a hidden place where a priest can disappear, and a place to keep the things needed for Mass. The woman of the house runs a butcher's shop with her husband. Her name is Margaret Clitherow. In the England of Elizabeth the First, sheltering a Catholic priest is a crime that can be punished by death. Earlier, a scholar from Oxford named Edmund Campion rode from house to house in disguise, saying Mass in homes like hers. Today, two English Catholics, and the hidden priests.
screen: `A KNOCK IN YORK.` → `A HIDDEN PLACE.` → `A SCHOLAR IN DISGUISE.`

segments.voice: First, the scholar. Edmund Campion was a brilliant Oxford man, admired at court. He became Catholic, joined the Jesuits abroad, and came back to England secretly, knowing what it might cost. He preached in private houses and moved on before he could be caught. In a letter to the queen's council, he wrote that the cost had been counted and the work begun, and could not be stopped. He was arrested, tortured, tried for treason, and executed. At his trial he argued that in condemning him, they condemned their own ancestors, whose faith he shared. Second, the hidden rooms. Catholic families built hiding places into their houses, so priests could vanish when searchers came. They're known as priest holes. Third, the butcher's wife. Margaret Clitherow hid priests in York. When she was arrested, she refused to enter a plea, so there would be no trial at which her children and household could be made to testify. For refusing, the law of the time had her crushed to death. Fourth, the honest frame. In that century, Christians of different churches put one another to death, in England and elsewhere. Protestants died under Catholic rulers too. The Church honors its martyrs, and in our own time has also asked forgiveness for violence done in its name. The Gospel that Campion and Clitherow held to says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are they that suffer persecution for justice' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."
screen: `CAMPION: THE COST IS COUNTED.` · `PRIEST HOLES.` · `MARGARET REFUSES TO PLEAD.` · `CHRISTIANS KILLING CHRISTIANS.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THEY THAT SUFFER PERSECUTION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for anyone persecuted for religion. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind people somewhere in the world today who are in danger for what they believe, or for what they don't. Any faith, any place. Don't pick sides. Just hold them: the ones hiding, the ones in prison, the families waiting for news. If you pray, you can pray for them, and for those who persecute them, as Jesus asked. If you don't, simply wish them safety and freedom. The bell holds the time.
Edmund Campion and Margaret Clitherow. A Jesuit scholar who came home in secret, and a butcher's wife in York who hid priests. Both died for their faith.
screen: `EDMUND CAMPION AND MARGARET CLITHEROW — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: hidden priests. Today, notice who in your world has to hide part of who they are to stay safe, and find one way to make your corner safer for them. Day eight hundred fifty-five.

856.title: Galileo, honestly (1633)
856.hook: the Church condemned Galileo; in 1992 John Paul II acknowledged the error
856.howItsDone: The Vatican keeps an observatory and a Pontifical Academy of Sciences, and Catholic teaching holds that faith and reason cannot truly contradict each other.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Edmund Campion, Margaret Clitherow, and the hidden places in their houses. Your line was hidden priests. Did you make a corner safer? Today, a story the Church tells against itself. Day eight hundred fifty-six.

A tube of glass and wood, pointed at the night sky over Italy. Through it, the moon has mountains. Jupiter has small lights circling it. The man at the eyepiece writes it all up in a short book with a Latin title, the Starry Messenger. He is a Catholic, a professor, and very sure of himself. What he's seeing points to an idea that the earth moves around the sun. Some in the Church will call that idea against the Scriptures. Today, honestly: Galileo.
screen: `MOUNTAINS ON THE MOON.` → `THE STARRY MESSENGER.` → `THE EARTH MOVES.`

segments.voice: First, the argument. Galileo's critics pointed to passages like the one where Joshua commands the sun to stand still. If the sun stands still, they said, it must normally move. Galileo answered in a long letter. He quoted a churchman of his day: the Holy Spirit means to teach us how one goes to heaven, not how the heavens go. Scripture, he argued, speaks the way ordinary people speak about sunrise. Second, the condemnation. The Holy Office in Rome ruled against the idea, and later put Galileo on trial. He was made to kneel and formally renounce the view that the earth moves. He spent the rest of his life confined to his house near Florence, and kept working. He was not burned, and he remained a Catholic. Third, the legend. People say that as he rose from his knees he muttered, and yet it moves. It's a good line. But it isn't in the trial records; it's a story told later. Fourth, the admission. Centuries later, Pope John Paul the Second asked for the case to be studied again. Speaking to the Pontifical Academy of Sciences, he acknowledged that the theologians who condemned Galileo had erred, and called the affair a tragic mutual misunderstanding. A pope had said, in public, that the condemnation was a mistake. Some Catholics pair this with the Psalm, in the Douay-Rheims: "The heavens shew forth the glory of God." For those who pray it, the Psalm and the telescope look at the same sky.
screen: `THE SUN STANDS STILL?` · `HOW TO GO TO HEAVEN, NOT HOW IT GOES.` · `CONDEMNED, CONFINED, STILL CATHOLIC.` · `AND YET IT MOVES: A LATER STORY.` · then, large: `THE ERROR, ADMITTED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: admit an error openly. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you got wrong, and haven't quite owned. A judgment you made about someone. An argument you won that you shouldn't have. Something you insisted on that turned out false. Let it be what it was. Then picture saying it plainly, to the person it touched: I was wrong about that. If you pray, you can bring it to God first. If you don't, simply practice the words. The bell holds the time.
Galileo. The Catholic astronomer whose telescope findings backed a moving earth, who was condemned in Rome, and whose case a pope later called an error.
Your line: the error, admitted. Today, if someone corrects you, thank them before you defend yourself, and check whether they're right. Day eight hundred fifty-six.

857.title: Matteo Ricci in China (1552–1610)
857.hook: a Jesuit who learned Chinese, dressed as a scholar and made friends
857.howItsDone: Catholic missionaries and bishops speak of inculturation when they bring the liturgy, music and art of a local culture into the life of the Church, and Ricci is often remembered in that conversation, especially by Jesuits.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Galileo, told honestly: a condemnation, and much later a pope saying out loud that the Church had erred. Your line was the error, admitted. Did you get a chance to admit one of your own? Day eight hundred fifty-seven.

An Italian with a long beard sits in a scholar's silk robe, in a city at the far end of the world from Rome, and his guests are not there to hear a sermon. They're there for his maps, his clocks, his mathematics, and his memory, which could do tricks they had never seen. They argue with him about Confucius. He argues back, in their language, quoting their classics. Some of them become his friends. A few become Christians. His name is Matteo Ricci, a Jesuit, and the long word for what he was trying to do is today's word.
screen: `A SCHOLAR'S SILK ROBE.` → `MAPS, CLOCKS, MEMORY.` → `ARGUING IN THEIR LANGUAGE.`

segments.voice: Inculturation means letting the faith take root in a culture, speaking its language and wearing its clothes, without stopping being itself. Ricci never used the word. It came much later. But his life is one of the stories Catholics reach for when they explain it. First, the language. Ricci and his companions studied Chinese for years, the spoken language and the written characters, until he could write books that Chinese scholars read seriously. Second, the clothes. At first the Jesuits dressed like Buddhist monks. Then Ricci noticed who was listening: the educated class who read Confucius. So he changed into the robes of a scholar. Third, friendship. One of his early books in Chinese was a small collection of sayings on friendship, drawn from Western writers. It said, in effect: I came a long way, and I came to be your friend. One of his friends, the scholar Xu Guangqi, became a Christian and worked with him on translating geometry. Fourth, the hard question. Ricci judged that honoring Confucius and the ancestors could be kept by Chinese Christians as a civil and family custom, not worship. Others in the Church disagreed, strongly. That argument went on long after his death, and Church rulings on it changed over time. So inculturation is not a slogan. It's a question you have to keep asking: what belongs to the faith, and what is simply the coat it happened to arrive in? Paul put the instinct behind it in one line, in the Douay-Rheims: "I became all things to all men, that I might save all."
screen: `FIRST, THE LANGUAGE.` · `FROM MONK'S ROBE TO SCHOLAR'S ROBE.` · `A BOOK ON FRIENDSHIP.` · `THE RITES: CUSTOM OR WORSHIP?` · then, large: `ALL THINGS TO ALL MEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn something about another culture, the way a friend would. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person you know whose family comes from somewhere you don't. A coworker, a neighbor, a classmate. What do you actually know about where they come from? A food, a holiday, a word? Notice where the knowing stops. Then pick one thing you'd like to ask them, not to study them, but because friends ask. If you pray, you can hold that person before God. If you don't, simply hold them in mind with curiosity. The bell holds the time.
Inculturation. The faith taking root in a culture, in its language and its clothes, while staying itself. Matteo Ricci, in a scholar's robe, is a story Catholics tell about it.
Your line: friendship first. Today, before you try to explain yourself to someone, ask them one real question about their world, and listen to the whole answer. Day eight hundred fifty-seven.

858.title: Rose of Lima (1586–1617)
858.hook: a young woman in a garden hut in Lima, remembered as the first canonized saint of the Americas
858.howItsDone: Catholics in Peru and across Latin America keep the feast of Saint Rose of Lima, often with processions, and some Dominican laypeople look to her as a model of holiness lived outside a convent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Matteo Ricci in a scholar's robe, and the long word inculturation. Your line was friendship first. Did you ask anyone a real question about their world? Day eight hundred fifty-eight.

At the back of a family garden in Lima, in Peru, there's a hut with barely room for one person. Inside, a young woman sews. Her needlework and the flowers she grows help keep her family fed. Some days the door opens onto a different job: sick and hungry people from the city, whom she brings into a room of her parents' house and nurses herself. She never enters a convent. She never travels. And yet the Church remembers her as the first person from the Americas to be named a saint. Her baptismal name was Isabel. In time she was called Rose.
screen: `A HUT IN A GARDEN.` → `NEEDLEWORK AND FLOWERS.` → `THE SICK IN HER PARENTS' HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Tradition says the name Rose came from a servant who saw her as a baby and thought her face looked like a rose. She kept it. First, a life at home. Rose wanted a life given to God, but she did not join an enclosed convent. She became a Dominican tertiary: a laywoman who follows the spirituality of the Dominicans while living in the world. Her cloister was a hut in her family's garden. Second, the work of her hands. She sewed and sold flowers to help her family, and she took the poor and sick into her parents' house and nursed them herself. Third, the hard part, and it should be told honestly. Rose practiced severe penances: fasting, sleeping on hard boards, wearing things meant to hurt. Her biographers wrote about these as heroic. Some Catholics today read them more carefully, as signs of a fierce love that should not be copied, and the Church does not ask anyone to imitate them. Fourth, the cross at the center. Rose's spirituality kept returning to the suffering Christ. Paul put it in one line, in the Douay-Rheims: "God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ." She belonged to a city full of new wealth and old wounds, the city of conquerors and of the conquered. When the Church later named her a saint, the Americas had their first. Lima still keeps her feast as its own.
screen: `A ROSE, NAMED BY A SERVANT.` · `A TERTIARY IN A GARDEN HUT.` · `FLOWERS, NEEDLEWORK, THE SICK.` · `PENANCES: TOLD HONESTLY.` · then, large: `SAVE IN THE CROSS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for Latin America, or hold it in mind. Settle, and breathe. Picture a map, from Mexico down to the far south. Let a few places rise: a city you've heard of, a country in the news, a family you know who comes from there. Rest on one. If you pray, you can ask Rose of Lima to pray for that place, or say a Hail Mary for its people. If you don't pray, simply hold them, the sick and the poor especially, the ones Rose brought into her parents' house. The bell holds the time.
Rose of Lima. A Dominican laywoman in a garden hut, who sewed, grew flowers and nursed the poor, remembered as the first saint of the Americas.

Your line: first of the americas. Today, when news from Latin America reaches you, let it be people before it is a headline, and name one of them, even just a city, in your heart. Day eight hundred fifty-eight.

859.title: Martin de Porres (1579–1639)
859.hook: a mixed-race Dominican brother in Lima, with a broom, a clinic, and mice he fed
859.howItsDone: Catholics often show Saint Martin de Porres with a broom, and some parishes and schools named for him run food pantries or outreach to the poor; he is invoked by people who face racial prejudice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rose of Lima in her garden hut, nursing the sick in her parents' house. Your line was first of the americas. Did you hold a place in Latin America for a breath? Today we stay in the same city. Day eight hundred fifty-nine.

A statue of him will often show the same things: a Dominican in a black and white habit, a dark-skinned face, and in his hand, not a book or a sword, but a broom. Sometimes there's a dog at his feet, a cat, and a mouse, all eating from one bowl. It looks like a children's picture. It's actually a summary of a life. He swept floors, cut hair, set bones, fed the hungry at the door, and for a long time held the lowest place in his house. Today, Martin de Porres.
screen: `NOT A BOOK, NOT A SWORD.` → `A BROOM.` → `A DOG, A CAT, A MOUSE.`

segments.voice: First, where he started. Martin was born in Lima, the son of a Spanish nobleman and a freed Black woman. His father did not acknowledge him at first. The colonial world sorted people by race, and Martin landed near the bottom. Second, the door that was half open. He trained as a barber, which in his day also meant small surgery and setting bones. Then he asked to join the Dominicans. The rules of the time kept men like him from taking full vows, so he entered as a donado, a lay helper who gave his work to the house. He swept. He cleaned. Only later did the community admit him as a professed brother. Third, the clinic. He became the infirmarian, caring for sick friars, and the care spread out the door: to slaves, to the poor of the city, to anyone who came. Fourth, the stories. Tradition says that when the priory was short of money, Martin offered to be sold to pay its debts. Tradition says he struck a deal with the mice in the house: stay in the garden, and I'll feed you there. Some of these are legends, retold many times; even so, they point one way. He took the lowest place and made it holy. Jesus describes himself in that place, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am in the midst of you, as he that serveth." The broom in his statues is not decoration. It's the claim his life makes: that sweeping a floor for God is not a lesser kind of prayer.
screen: `A NOBLEMAN'S SON, NOT ACKNOWLEDGED.` · `A DONADO: THE LOWEST PLACE.` · `THE CLINIC OUT THE DOOR.` · `SELL ME. FEED THE MICE.` · then, large: `AS HE THAT SERVETH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do a humble job gladly. Settle, and breathe. Think of one small chore waiting for you today, the kind nobody thanks anyone for. Dishes, a trash bag, a floor, an inbox. Picture yourself doing it, slowly, without hurrying to be done. Notice whether something in you says this is beneath me. Let that voice speak, then let it pass. If you pray, you can offer the chore to God before you start. If you don't, simply decide to do it well. The bell holds the time.
Martin de Porres. A mixed-race Dominican brother of Lima, a barber and nurse, who took the lowest place in his house and made it a place of care.
Your line: the saint with a broom. Today, pick up one job someone else would skip, and do it as if it mattered, because to someone it does. Day eight hundred fifty-nine.

860.title: Peter Claver (1580–1654)
860.hook: in Cartagena he met every slave ship and called himself the slave of the slaves
860.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Peter Claver and invoke him as a patron of enslaved people and of ministry to African-descended communities; some parishes mark it with prayer for victims of human trafficking.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Martin de Porres, the brother in Lima who swept floors and nursed the city's poor. Your line was the saint with a broom. What humble job did you pick up? Today the story moves north, to the Caribbean. Day eight hundred sixty.

Word comes into the port of Cartagena that a ship has been sighted. For the merchants, that means cargo. For the people in the hold, it means the end of a voyage they were forced to make in chains, sick, starving, some of them dying. And for one Spanish Jesuit, it means he goes down to the docks with baskets of food, water, lemons and medicine, and climbs down into the hold. This is a hard story, and it should be told plainly. Today, Peter Claver.
screen: `A SHIP IS SIGHTED.` → `PEOPLE IN CHAINS IN THE HOLD.` → `A PRIEST CLIMBS DOWN.`

segments.voice: First, the place. Cartagena, on the Caribbean coast of what is now Colombia, was a port where enslaved Africans were brought and sold. Claver, a Spanish Jesuit, was sent there as a young man. Before he left Spain, an elderly Jesuit brother, Alphonsus Rodriguez, a doorkeeper, had urged him toward the people no one cared for. Second, the docks. When a ship came in, Claver went aboard and below decks. He brought food and water first, and washed and bandaged the sick. He used interpreters to speak to people in their own languages. He taught and baptized those who asked. He followed them into the yards where they were held, and later visited them on plantations and in hospitals. Third, the vow. When he made his final vows as a Jesuit, he signed his name with a phrase in Latin: the slave of the Africans forever. The saying passed down as slave of the slaves. Fourth, the honest part. Claver did not end the slave trade, and the Church of his day did not condemn it outright. He served inside an evil he could not stop, and those who tell his story now try to remember both: his love, and the system it ran into. Jesus's words in Matthew's Gospel read like the job description he took on, in the Douay-Rheims: "I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me to drink." Near the end of his life Claver was sick and largely forgotten, cared for poorly himself. The Church later named him a saint, and Catholics invoke him as a patron of enslaved people.
screen: `CARTAGENA: A SLAVE PORT.` · `DOWN INTO THE HOLD.` · `SLAVE OF THE AFRICANS FOREVER.` · `HE COULDN'T STOP IT. HE SERVED.` · then, large: `I WAS HUNGRY, AND YOU GAVE ME TO EAT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for victims of slavery today, or hold them in mind. Settle, and breathe. Forced labor did not end with the ships. People are still trafficked, held in debt, made to work without pay or freedom, sometimes close to where you live. You don't need names. Let them be present, the way the people in the hold were present to Claver. If you pray, you can ask Peter Claver to pray for them, or pray an Our Father slowly. If you don't, simply stay with them, and let it cost you a little. The bell holds the time.
Peter Claver. A Spanish Jesuit in Cartagena who met the slave ships with food and medicine, and called himself the slave of the Africans forever.
Your line: slave of the slaves. Today, before you buy something, pause for one breath and remember the hands that made it. Day eight hundred sixty.

861.title: Kateri Tekakwitha (1656–1680)
861.hook: a Mohawk and Algonquin woman, scarred by smallpox, later named a saint
861.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Kateri Tekakwitha, and her shrines in New York and Quebec draw pilgrims; Indigenous Catholic gatherings in North America often bear her name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter Claver, climbing down into the holds of slave ships with food and water. Your line was slave of the slaves. This week walked from hidden priests in England and Galileo's trial to Ricci in China, then Lima and Cartagena. Today it ends in the forests of the north. Day eight hundred sixty-one.

A girl in a Mohawk village keeps a blanket pulled over her head when she goes outside. Smallpox swept through when she was small. It took her parents and left her face marked and her eyes weak, so bright light hurts. Her mother had been an Algonquin Christian. Her father was Mohawk. She grows up in her uncle's longhouse, quiet, skilled with her hands, and saying no to the marriage her family wants for her. Then black-robed priests come to the village. Today, Kateri Tekakwitha.
screen: `A BLANKET OVER HER HEAD.` → `SMALLPOX TOOK HER PARENTS.` → `SHE SAYS NO TO MARRIAGE.`

segments.voice: First, two peoples in one person. Kateri's father was Mohawk, her mother Algonquin, and she carried both. Catholics remember her today as a saint of Indigenous North America, and some Indigenous Catholics speak of her as one of their own, not as someone the missionaries made. Second, baptism. She asked a Jesuit, Jacques de Lamberville, to teach her, and he baptized her. She took the name Catherine. Kateri is the Mohawk way of saying it. Some in her village turned on her. The early accounts tell of mockery and threats, some of it because she refused to work on Sundays. Third, the journey. She left, on foot and by canoe, for a Christian mission village near Montreal, where Mohawk and other Native Christians lived together. There she prayed long hours, cared for the sick and old, and made a promise to God never to marry. Her penances were severe, and she was never strong. She died young. Fourth, the lily. The Jesuits who knew her wrote her life, and one of them recorded that after she died, the scars on her face faded. Catholics hand it down as his testimony, an eyewitness's word. The Church named her Venerable, then Blessed, then a saint. People call her the Lily of the Mohawks, and some Catholics hear in that name a line from the Song of Songs, in the Douay-Rheims: "As the lily among thorns, so is my love among the daughters." A lily, growing where it was not expected to.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for Indigenous Catholics, or keep them in your thoughts a while. Settle, and breathe. Across the Americas there are Native communities who keep the faith in their own languages, with their own songs and their own memories, some of them painful. Let one come to mind, a nation whose land you live on, a reservation you've driven past, a name you've heard. If you pray, you can ask Kateri Tekakwitha to pray for them. If you don't, simply hold them with respect. And if this week's stories have been heavy, let yourself rest here. The bell holds the time.
Kateri Tekakwitha. A Mohawk and Algonquin woman, scarred by smallpox, baptized against her village's wishes, who walked to a mission and gave her life to prayer and the sick.
Your line: lily of the mohawks. Today, learn the name of the people who first lived on the land you're standing on, and say it once. This week ends here. Day eight hundred sixty-one.
